content: Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) is an extensive and structured vocabulary system designed to facilitate the indexing of journal articles and books in the life sciences. It is developed and maintained by the United States National Library of Medicine (NLM). MeSH is utilized by the MEDLINE/PubMed database for indexing articles and by the NLM catalog for organizing book holdings. The MeSH database is freely accessible online, and its printed version was discontinued in 2007. When articles are indexed in MEDLINE/PubMed, they are assigned approximately 10-15 MeSH headings or subheadings. Among these, one or two are designated as major topics and are marked with an asterisk. During a PubMed search, entry terms are automatically mapped to their corresponding MeSH descriptors. Additionally, the search includes all descriptors hierarchically subordinate to the selected term by default. The 2005 version of MeSH includes 22,568 subject headings, also referred to as descriptors. Each descriptor is typically accompanied by a concise definition, links to related descriptors, and a list of synonyms or closely related terms, known as entry terms. This synonym list allows MeSH to function as a thesaurus as well. Descriptors in MeSH are organized hierarchically, and a single descriptor may appear in multiple locations within the hierarchy. Each location is assigned a systematic label called a tree number. For instance, the descriptor Digestive System Neoplasms is represented by the tree number C06.301 under Digestive System Diseases (C06) and also by C04.588.274 under Neoplasms by Site (C04.588). These tree numbers may change as MeSH is updated, but each descriptor is also assigned a unique alphanumeric ID that remains constant. Most descriptors include a brief explanatory text written by the MeSH team, based on standard reference sources such as encyclopedias and textbooks. These descriptions do not provide specific citations for individual statements but instead refer readers to a general bibliography. MeSH also includes qualifiers, which are standardized subheadings that can be added to descriptors to refine the topic. For example, the descriptor Measles can be combined with the qualifier epidemiology to create Measles/epidemiology, which refers to articles on the epidemiology of measles. There are 83 qualifiers in total, but not all descriptor/qualifier combinations are valid, as some may lack meaningful context. In addition to descriptors, MeSH contains approximately 139,000 Supplementary Concept Records. These records are not part of the controlled vocabulary used for indexing MEDLINE articles but serve to expand the thesaurus. Many of these records describe chemical substances and include links to the most relevant descriptors for MEDLINE searches. MeSH has been translated into multiple languages, enabling the retrieval of documents in various languages. The top-level categories in the MeSH descriptor hierarchy include Anatomy, Organisms, Diseases, Chemicals and Drugs, Analytical, Diagnostic and Therapeutic Techniques and Equipment, Psychiatry and Psychology, Biological Sciences, Physical Sciences, Anthropology, Education, Sociology and Social Phenomena, Technology and Food and Beverages, Humanities, Information Science, Persons, Health Care, Publication Characteristics, and Geographic Locations. Each category is further subdivided into more specific topics, providing a comprehensive framework for organizing biomedical and life sciences information.
